title: What Is a Mineral?
description: Defining the building blocks of all rocks

concepts.title: The Five Criteria
concepts.contentHtml:
A mineral is not just any rock or crystal. Scientists use five strict criteria: a mineral must be naturally occurring, inorganic, solid, have a definite chemical composition, and have an ordered crystalline structure.

Ice qualifies — it forms naturally, is a solid with the formula H₂O, and has a crystalline lattice. Coal does not — it is organic (formed from ancient life). Synthetic diamonds fail the 'naturally occurring' test, even though they are pure carbon arranged identically to natural diamonds.

concepts.title: Common Rock-Forming Minerals
concepts.contentHtml:
Only about 30 minerals make up the bulk of Earth's crust. The most abundant are the silicates — built around silicon-oxygen tetrahedra.

Key examples:
— Quartz (SiO₂): glassy, very hard, found in granite and sandstone.
— Feldspars (KAlSi₃O₈ etc.): most abundant mineral group in the crust.
— Micas (biotite, muscovite): sheet silicates that split into thin flakes.
— Olivine (Mg,Fe)₂SiO₄: major component of the upper mantle.

Recognising these minerals in hand specimens is the first skill of every field geologist.

concepts.title: Identifying Minerals
concepts.contentHtml:
Geologists identify minerals using physical properties:

  • Colour — useful but unreliable (quartz comes in many colours).
  • Streak — the colour of the powdered mineral on a white tile; more consistent than surface colour.
  • Lustre — metallic (pyrite), vitreous (quartz), pearly (mica).
  • Cleavage — how a mineral breaks along crystal planes (mica splits into perfect sheets).
  • Hardness — resistance to scratching, measured on the Mohs scale from 1 (talc) to 10 (diamond).

A combination of these properties is usually enough to identify any common mineral in the field.

title: The Mohs Hardness Scale
description: How geologists rank the scratch resistance of minerals

concepts.title: From Talc to Diamond
concepts.contentHtml:
Friedrich Mohs devised his hardness scale in 1812, ranking ten reference minerals from softest (1) to hardest (10):

1 Talc · 2 Gypsum · 3 Calcite · 4 Fluorite · 5 Apatite · 6 Orthoclase · 7 Quartz · 8 Topaz · 9 Corundum · 10 Diamond

The scale is ordinal, not linear — diamond (10) is not twice as hard as corundum (9). It is actually about four times harder. The jumps in absolute hardness are uneven, but the ordering reliably predicts which mineral will scratch which.

concepts.title: Field Tests for Hardness
concepts.contentHtml:
Field geologists use convenient proxies:

  • A fingernail scratches minerals up to hardness ~2.5 (gypsum but not calcite).
  • A copper coin scratches up to ~3.5.
  • A steel knife blade scratches up to ~5.5.
  • Window glass has hardness ~5.5–6.
  • Quartz (7) scratches glass easily.

By systematically testing what scratches what, you can bracket an unknown mineral to a Mohs value without any specialist equipment — crucial when working in remote terrain.

concepts.title: Why Hardness Matters
concepts.contentHtml:
Hardness reflects the strength of chemical bonds in the crystal lattice. Diamond is the hardest natural substance because each carbon atom forms four strong covalent bonds in a tetrahedral arrangement — the densest bonding network possible.

Hardness has immense practical importance:
— Corundum (9) — the mineral of rubies and sapphires — is used industrially as an abrasive.
— Talc (1) is so soft it feels greasy, making it ideal for cosmetics and lubricants.
— Quartz sand (7) is hard enough to abrade metals, causing wear in industrial machinery.

title: Crystal Systems and Growth
description: How atomic order becomes visible geometry

concepts.title: The Seven Crystal Systems
concepts.contentHtml:
All mineral crystals belong to one of seven crystal systems, defined by the symmetry of their unit cell (the smallest repeating arrangement of atoms):

  • Cubic — equal axes at 90° (halite, garnet, diamond).
  • Tetragonal — two equal, one different, 90° (zircon).
  • Orthorhombic — three unequal axes at 90° (olivine, topaz).
  • Hexagonal — four axes; six-fold symmetry (quartz, calcite, beryl).
  • Trigonal — three-fold symmetry, often grouped with hexagonal (tourmaline).
  • Monoclinic — one oblique angle (gypsum, micas).
  • Triclinic — no right angles (plagioclase feldspar).

concepts.title: How Crystals Grow
concepts.contentHtml:
Crystals form when atoms arrange themselves into ordered lattices as a melt or solution cools. The slower the cooling, the larger the crystals — there is more time for atoms to find their preferred positions.

This is why:

  • Granite (slow-cooling magma deep underground) has large, visible crystals.
  • Basalt (fast-cooling lava at the surface) has microscopic crystals.
  • Obsidian (near-instant quench) has no crystals at all — it is volcanic glass.

The world's largest known crystals — selenite crystals up to 11 m long — grew in the Cave of Crystals in Naica, Mexico, from hydrothermal fluids over ~500,000 years.

concepts.title: Polymorphs — Same Chemistry, Different Structure
concepts.contentHtml:
The same chemical formula can produce completely different minerals depending on temperature and pressure. These are called polymorphs.

The most famous example is carbon:
— Graphite: carbon atoms in flat sheets, weakly bonded together — soft, grey, used in pencils.
— Diamond: carbon atoms in a 3-D tetrahedral lattice — the hardest natural material, transparent.

Another example is aluminium silicate:
— Kyanite, sillimanite, and andalusite all have the formula Al₂SiO₅ but form at different pressures and temperatures, making them useful as geothermometers and geobarometers for reading the conditions of ancient metamorphic events.

title: Gems and Ore Minerals
description: The minerals humans covet most — and why

concepts.title: What Makes a Gemstone?
concepts.contentHtml:
A gemstone is any mineral (or occasionally organic material like pearl or amber) that is beautiful, durable, and rare enough to be valued for adornment.

Beauty — colour, transparency, and optical effects like the 'fire' of diamond (splitting white light into spectral colours).
Durability — hardness (≥7 for most gems) and resistance to cleavage.
Rarity — supply relative to demand.

The 'big four' precious gemstones are diamond, ruby (red corundum), sapphire (blue corundum), and emerald (green beryl). Ruby and sapphire are the same mineral — corundum (Al₂O₃) — coloured by trace impurities of chromium or iron/titanium respectively.

concepts.title: Where Gems Form
concepts.contentHtml:
Different geological environments produce different gems:

  • Diamonds crystallise in the deep mantle under enormous pressure and are brought to the surface in explosive volcanic pipes called kimberlites.
  • Rubies and sapphires form in metamorphic rocks and are often found in river gravels after erosion — the famous sapphire deposits of Sri Lanka and Kashmir formed this way.
  • Emeralds grow in hydrothermal veins where beryllium-rich fluids interact with chromium-bearing host rock — an unusually specific combination explaining their rarity.
  • Opals form when silica-rich water fills voids in rock and the gel dries — Australia produces 95 % of the world's opals.

concepts.title: Ore Minerals and Economic Geology
concepts.contentHtml:
An ore mineral is one from which a valuable element can be economically extracted. The most important metallic ore minerals include:

  • Magnetite and hematite (iron ores) — basis of the steel industry.
  • Chalcopyrite (copper iron sulfide) — the world's primary copper ore.
  • Galena (lead sulfide) — the main lead ore; historically also the main source of silver.
  • Sphalerite (zinc sulfide) — principal zinc ore.
  • Native gold — forms in hydrothermal quartz veins and alluvial placers.

Ore deposits form through hydrothermal, magmatic, or sedimentary concentration processes — geology literally underlies the entire materials economy.

title: Minerals and the Planet
description: From critical minerals for technology to clues about other worlds

concepts.title: Critical Minerals for the Energy Transition
concepts.contentHtml:
The shift to renewable energy and electric vehicles depends on minerals that were previously niche:
— Lithium (spodumene, lithium brines) — lithium-ion batteries.
— Cobalt (cobaltite) — battery cathodes; 70 % of supply from the DRC.
— Rare-earth elements (bastnäsite, monazite) — permanent magnets in wind turbines and EV motors.
— Graphite — battery anodes.

Mineral supply chains are now a geopolitical concern. Understanding mineralogy and ore deposit geology is essential for securing resources needed to decarbonize civilization.

concepts.title: Minerals as Time Capsules
concepts.contentHtml:
Minerals record the conditions under which they formed — and that information survives for billions of years.

Zircon (ZrSiO₄) is the champion. It incorporates uranium but not lead at crystallisation, so uranium-lead ratios measure age precisely. The oldest minerals on Earth are zircon grains from Jack Hills, Australia — 4.4 billion years old, predating the oldest known rocks.

Fluid inclusions trapped in mineral grains preserve samples of ancient seawater or hydrothermal fluids. Mineral assemblages in meteorites reveal conditions in the early Solar System. Mineralogy is planetary science as much as Earth science.

concepts.title: New Minerals and the Deep Carbon Cycle
concepts.contentHtml:
Mineralogy is still a frontier. Scientists discover roughly 100 new mineral species per year — most from deep-Earth samples or exotic environments. As of 2024 over 6,000 minerals are officially recognised by the International Mineralogical Association.

The deep carbon cycle involves carbon stored in minerals (as carbonates, diamonds, and organic-rich sediments) cycling between the surface and mantle over millions of years. Carbonate minerals like calcite and dolomite lock up vast amounts of CO₂ and release it through metamorphism and volcanism. Understanding this cycle is crucial for modelling long-term climate over Earth's history.

title: Composition of Earth's Crust
description: How much of each mineral and element makes up the rocks beneath our feet

concepts.title: The Eight Dominant Elements
concepts.contentHtml:
By mass, just eight elements account for over 98 % of Earth's continental crust:

  • Oxygen — 46.6 %
  • Silicon — 27.7 %
  • Aluminium — 8.1 %
  • Iron — 5.0 %
  • Calcium — 3.6 %
  • Sodium — 2.8 %
  • Potassium — 2.6 %
  • Magnesium — 2.1 %

Everything else — including all the metals we mine industrially (copper, zinc, lead, tin, gold, the rare earths) — together makes up less than 2 %. This dramatic skew is why ore-forming geological processes that concentrate trace elements are so economically important.

concepts.title: Mineral Group Abundances
concepts.contentHtml:
By volume, the crust is overwhelmingly silicate:

  • Feldspars — about 51 % of the crust by volume; the single most abundant mineral group. Plagioclase (~39 %) and alkali feldspar (~12 %).
  • Quartz — about 12 %.
  • Pyroxenes — about 11 %.
  • Amphiboles — about 5 %.
  • Micas — about 5 %.
  • Clays — about 5 %.
  • Other silicates (olivine, garnets, epidotes) — about 8 %.
  • Non-silicates (carbonates, oxides, sulfides, halides, sulfates) — about 8 % combined.

The takeaway: more than 90 % of the rock you ever step on is one of about a dozen silicate species.

concepts.title: Crust vs. Mantle vs. Core
concepts.contentHtml:
The crust is only 1 % of Earth's mass. The full picture is very different:

  • Inner and outer core (32 % of mass) — mostly iron and nickel.
  • Mantle (67 % of mass) — dominated by olivine, pyroxenes, and high-pressure silicates like ringwoodite and bridgmanite. Bridgmanite ((Mg,Fe)SiO₃) is in fact the most abundant mineral on Earth — by mass, it makes up about 38 % of the entire planet — but it only exists at lower-mantle pressures and was not formally named until 2014, after a sample was identified in a meteorite.
  • Crust — the silicate-feldspar zone we mine and live on.

So the most abundant mineral on Earth is one no human has ever held in pristine form at the surface — outside of meteorite samples, it decompresses and changes structure on its way up.

title: Minerals Beyond Earth
description: Asteroids, the Moon, Mars, and the case for space mining

concepts.title: Three Classes of Asteroid
concepts.contentHtml:
Asteroids are sorted by spectral type into three broad groups, each with very different mineralogies:

  • C-type (carbonaceous) — about 75 % of known asteroids. Dark, primitive, rich in hydrated clays, organics, and water ice. Key targets for water and life-precursor chemistry; Bennu (visited by OSIRIS-REx) and Ryugu (visited by Hayabusa2) are C-types.
  • S-type (silicaceous) — about 17 %. Stony, dominated by olivine and pyroxene, often with native iron and nickel. Eros and Itokawa are S-types.
  • M-type (metallic) — about 8 %. Thought to be exposed cores of differentiated proto-planets. Dominated by iron-nickel metal. 16 Psyche, the largest M-type, is the target of NASA's Psyche mission (launched 2023).

concepts.title: Why Space Mining Is Tempting
concepts.contentHtml:
Earth's economically accessible deposits of platinum-group metals (PGMs — platinum, palladium, iridium, rhodium, osmium, ruthenium) are concentrated in only a few large impact-related ore bodies, like the Bushveld Complex in South Africa.

Most of Earth's primordial PGMs sank into the core during planetary differentiation. Asteroids — especially M-types — never differentiated fully, so PGM concentrations there can be hundreds of times higher than the richest terrestrial ores. A single 1 km M-type asteroid is estimated to contain more platinum than has ever been mined on Earth.

Whether extracting them ever becomes economic depends on launch cost, propellant infrastructure, and the price of metals on Earth — a moving target.

concepts.title: Lunar and Martian Mineralogy
concepts.contentHtml:
The Moon is mineralogically simpler than Earth: dominantly anorthositic plagioclase in the lighter highlands, basalt in the dark maria. Apollo samples revealed three lunar-only minerals: armalcolite (named for the Apollo 11 crew Armstrong-Aldrin-Collins), tranquillityite, and pyroxferroite — though all three were later found in trace amounts on Earth.

Mars hosts widespread basalts plus extensive evidence of past water — clays, sulfates (including jarosite, ferrihydrite, and gypsum), and hematite spherules ('blueberries') discovered by the Opportunity rover. The presence of these hydrated minerals is one of the strongest indicators that liquid water flowed on the Martian surface for hundreds of millions of years.

Mineralogy, in short, is not just an Earth science. Reading the minerals on another world reveals its temperature, water history, and even the chance it once hosted life.
